secs.t: Company rule — Regulating Act 1773 to Charter Act 1853 · Revision points (14)

The
Regulating Act, 1773
set up the first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta (it began in 1774).
The Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the first Governor-General of India.

The first Supreme Court at Fort William opened in 1774 with Sir Elijah Impey as first Chief Justice; Macaulay was the first Law Member; Section 87 of the Charter Act, 1833 opened Company service to Indians without discrimination of religion or colour.
The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council for the first time.
Under the Regulating Act, 1773 the Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal, and
Warren Hastings
was the first.
The
Charter Act, 1853
introduced open competition for the Civil Services.
The Charter Act was enacted in 1813.
Regulating Act 1773 – Supreme Court at Calcutta; Pitt's India Act 1784 – Dual Control; Charter Act 1813 – monopoly partly abolished; Charter Act 1833 – Company lost its commercial role entirely.
The Regulating Act banned private trade.
The Act of 1786 empowered the Governor-General to override his Council.
Lord Cornwallis
was the first to exercise the powers granted by the Act of 1786.
The
Charter Act, 1833
ended the Company's trade monopoly completely and made it a purely administrative body.
The Board of Control handled political affairs under Dual Control.

Regulating Act, 1773 – Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal; Charter Act, 1833 – Bentinck as Governor-General of India; Charter Act, 1853 – enacted in 1853; 1858 Act – office of Viceroy (Canning).

secs.t: Crown rule — Act of 1858 and the Indian Councils Acts · Revision points (16)

x: Source:

Charter Act 1853 – open competition for Civil Services; 1858 Act – Canning as first Viceroy; 1909 Act – separate electorate for Muslims; 1919 Act – direct elections.
The Indian Councils Act, 1909 first associated Indians with the Executive Councils of the Viceroy and the Governors, and S.P. Sinha became the first Indian Law Member of the Viceroy's Council.

The 1909 Act is the Morley-Minto reforms, Lord Minto the 'Father of Communal Electorate', the 1919 Act the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms, and the separate electorate for Muslims a feature of the 1909 Act.
The
Government of India Act, 1858
transferred rule from the Company to the Crown and made the Governor-General the Viceroy.
Charter Act 1813, Indian Councils Act 1909, Government of India Act 1919, Government of India Act 1935: B, C, D, A.
The 1858 Act made Canning Viceroy, abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors, and created the Secretary of State for India with a 15-member Council.
The Indian Councils Act was enacted in 1861.
The 1861 Act restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras, a step towards decentralisation.
The
Indian Councils Act, 1861
gave the Viceroy power to issue Ordinances (and introduced the portfolio system).
A Viceroy's Ordinance under the 1861 Act could stay in force for up to
six months
The Indian Councils Act was enacted in 1892.
Existing High Courts continued under the Indian Councils Act of 1909.
The High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were established in 1862.
The Charter Act of 1833 added a Law Member.
The Indian Councils Act of 1892 introduced the principle of limited indirect election.
Charter Act, 1813 – ₹1 lakh education grant; Indian Councils Act, 1861 – portfolio system; Morley-Minto, 1909 – separate electorate for Muslims; 1935 Act – Federal Court (1 October 1937).

secs.t: Government of India Acts, 1919 and 1935 · Revision points (14)

x: Source:
Indian Polity – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #1 (pp 2-6), #22 (pp 52-55), #43 (pp 114-117)
The 1919 Act first made the Central Legislature bicameral, introduced dyarchy in the provinces and used the term 'responsible government'.
The 1935 Act provided for an All-India Federation, which never came into being, and dyarchy at the Centre, which was never implemented.

The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and set up the Federal Court, inaugurated on 1 October 1937 with Sir Maurice Gwyer as its first Chief Justice; the Supreme Court replaced it on 26 January 1950.
The Government of India Act of 1935 created Sindh as a new province.
Under the 1935 Act residuary powers were vested in
the Governor-General
— not in the Federal Court, the Executive Council or the provincial Governors.
The Chamber of Princes had 120 members, was created under the Government of India Act, 1919, and its first Chancellor was Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner.
The PAC was first set up in 1921 under the 1919 Act; the Federal Court was established under the 1935 Act; Sir Maurice Gwyer was its first Chief Justice.
The first NHRC Chairman took office in 1993; the first Law Commission of independent India dates from 1955; the Public Service Commission was provided by the 1919 Act and set up on 1 October 1926.
The Indian Independence Act was enacted in 1947.
1909 Act – supplementary questions allowed; S.P. Sinha – first Indian on the Viceroy's Executive Council; 1919 Act – Chamber of Princes; 1935 Act – Maurice Gwyer as Federal Court Chief Justice.
The 1919 Act is the
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
; the Morley-Minto Reforms were the 1909 Act.
The Government of India Act of 1935 provided the basis for the President’s Ordinance Power under Article 123.
The Indian Councils Act of 1909 did not introduce dyarchy.
1919 Act – bicameralism at the Centre; 1935 Act – Federal Court (1937); 1909 Act – separate electorates for Muslims; 1858 Act – rule passed to the Crown.

First meeting (9 Dec 1946), Objectives Resolution moved (13 Dec 1946), adopted (22 Jan 1947), Constitution adopted (26 Nov 1949): B, C, D, A. A resolution is moved before it is adopted, which rules out A and D.

M.N. Roy first put forward the idea (1934); the Swaraj Party made the first formal demand at its Ranchi conference, held in May 1934; the Assembly was constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946.

Sachchidananda Sinha presided temporarily at the first meeting, Rajendra Prasad became permanent President on 11 December 1946, Frank Anthony was the first temporary Deputy Chairman and H.C. Mukherjee the first permanent Vice-President.
B.N. Rau prepared the first draft of the Constitution as Constitutional Advisor.
The Constituent Assembly had 15 women members.
The Interim Government was announced on 24 August 1946.
The Constitution of India Bill of 1895 contained the first explicit demand for Fundamental Rights.

G.V. Mavalankar was the first Lok Sabha Speaker; Vithalbhai Patel was the first elected President of the Central Legislative Assembly (1925); Rajendra Prasad was the Constituent Assembly's permanent President and Sachchidananda Sinha its temporary President.
The Indian Independence Act was enacted in 1947.
First meeting of the Assembly (9 Dec 1946), National Flag adopted (22 Jul 1947), Constitution adopted (26 Nov 1949), in force (26 Jan 1950): B, A, C, D. The flag was adopted before Independence.
Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the Objective Resolution on
13 December 1946
The Indian Independence Act ended British rule.
The Drafting Committee under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was set up on
29 August 1947
26 November is observed as Constitution Day.

The 42nd Amendment is known as the Mini-Constitution.
The 52nd Amendment enacted the Anti-Defection Law.
The 73rd Amendment was enacted in 1992.
The 44th Amendment was enacted in 1978.
The 52nd Amendment amended Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191 to bring in disqualification on grounds of defection.
The 91st Amendment was enacted in 2003.
The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX, Articles 243–243O, with a three-tier Panchayati Raj; the 74th (1992) added Part IXA, Articles 243P–243ZG, for Municipalities.
42nd Amendment – 1976; 84th – 2001; 86th – 2002; its main insertion – the eleventh Fundamental Duty (Article 51A(k)), along with Article 21A.

The Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act removed the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights.
The 99th Amendment (2014) created the NJAC, struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.
1st Amendment – Ninth Schedule, Articles 31A, 31B and 15(4); 73rd – Panchayats and Eleventh Schedule; 74th – Municipalities and Twelfth Schedule; 103rd – EWS reservation.
The 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House's strength (and tightened anti-defection).
86th – Right to Education (6–14 years); 91st – 15% cap on ministries; 101st – GST; 106th – one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
The 103rd Amendment (2019) gave 10% reservation to Economically Weaker Sections.
The One Hundred and First Constitutional Amendment Act introduced the Goods and Services Tax.
The First Amendment (1951) dealt with agrarian reforms, the 42nd was enacted in 1976, and the 44th (1978) put 'armed rebellion' in place of 'internal disturbance' as a ground for Emergency.
The lowering of the voting age from 21 to 18 (61st Amendment) came into effect on
28 March 1989
The Panchayat provisions were enforced on 24 April 1993.
52nd Amendment (anti-defection) – 1985; 61st (voting age 18) – 1988, in force March 1989; 99th (NJAC) – 2014; 106th (women's reservation) – 2023.
The One Hundred and First Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 2016.

secs.t: Demand for a Constituent Assembly and its composition · Revision points (9)

x: Source:
Indian Polity – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #5 (pp 14-16)
M.N. Roy
first put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly in 1934.
The elections were held in July–August 1946, not June–July.
The Constituent Assembly was elected indirectly by Provincial Legislative Assemblies.
389 seats were planned (296 for British India, 93 for the Princely States), one member per 10 lakh population, and the Assembly had 15 women members.

The Swaraj Party made the first formal demand at Ranchi (May 1934), the Congress officially demanded a Constituent Assembly in 1935, Nehru declared for it in 1938, and the August Offer of 1940 accepted the principle.
The Cripps Mission made the final proposal for an elected Constituent Assembly in 1942.
Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League 73 and others 15, and the Assembly was not elected on adult franchise.
The Constituent Assembly election used restricted franchise under the Government of India Act 1935.
The Princely States started joining the Constituent Assembly from its third session in April 1947.

secs.t: Office-bearers, timeline and committees · Revision points (12)

Nehru chaired the Union Constitution Committee, Sardar Patel the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal Areas, J.B. Kripalani the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee and Dr. Rajendra Prasad the Steering Committee.
The Objectives Resolution was moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947; the Drafting Committee was formed on 29 August 1947 and the Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad chaired three of them: the Steering Committee, the Rules of Procedure Committee and the ad-hoc Flag Committee.
B.N. Rau was the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly.
The first meeting was on 9 December 1946 with Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha as Temporary (Provisional) President, and Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected Permanent President on 11 December 1946.

The Constitution was adopted on the last day of the eleventh session, signed at the last meeting on 24 January 1950, came into force on 26 January 1950, and the work took 2 years, 11 months and 17 days.
The Assembly held 11 sessions over 165 sitting days, and its final meeting was on 24 January 1950.
Frank Anthony was the first temporary Deputy Chairman of the Constituent Assembly.
The Drafting Committee had six other members besides its Chairman.
All six were the other members of the Drafting Committee: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B.L. Mitter and D.P. Khaitan.
N. Madhava Rao later replaced B.L. Mitter on the Drafting Committee.
Jawaharlal Nehru chaired the States Committee.

secs.t: Sources of the Constitution — borrowed features · Revision points (15)

x: Source:
Indian Polity – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #3 (pp 12-14)
Parliamentary government came from Britain, DPSP from Ireland, a federation with a strong Centre from Canada and the Concurrent List from Australia.
The procedure established by law was borrowed from Japan.
The Fundamental Duties were borrowed from the USSR.
Judicial review was borrowed from the USA.
The Government of India Act, 1935 provided the structural and administrative backbone.
The Cabinet system was borrowed from Britain, along with parliamentary government and the Rule of Law.
Single citizenship came from Britain, impeachment of the President from the USA, the method of electing the President from Ireland and the joint sitting of both Houses from Australia.
All three came from the USA: Fundamental Rights, independence of the judiciary and impeachment of the President.
The nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from Ireland.
The residuary powers with the Centre were borrowed from Canada.
Three: joint sitting, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and the language of the Preamble came from Australia.
The election of members of the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from
South Africa
The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble were borrowed from France.
The federal scheme was associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.
Part I – the Union and its Territory; Part II – Citizenship; Part V – the Union (executive, Parliament, judiciary); Part XX – Amendment of the Constitution.

Part I was part of the original Constitution.

Article 1 says India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States.
Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void.
Article 14 provides equality before law.
Article 37 makes DPSP non-justiciable but fundamental in governance, Article 43A covers workers' participation in management, and Article 50 separates the judiciary from the executive.
Equal justice and free legal aid – Article 39A; humane conditions of work – Article 42; Uniform Civil Code – Article 44; environment – Article 48A.
Three: Articles 14, 21 and 32 are Fundamental Rights (Part III).
Article 21A
(added by the 86th Amendment, 2002) makes education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6–14.
Article 12 defines 'State'; Article 15 prohibits discrimination; Article 16 gives equality of opportunity in public employment; Article 18 abolishes titles.
Article 15 permits special provisions.

Article 20 protects in respect of conviction; Article 22 against arrest and detention; Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits employment of children in factories.

Article 21A – Right to Education (86th Amendment); Articles 25–28 – freedom of religion; Articles 29–30 – minorities' cultural and educational rights; Article 32 – constitutional remedies, Ambedkar's 'heart and soul'.
Articles 33 to 35 concern the power to modify Fundamental Rights for forces and related groups.
Article 38 – social order and welfare; Article 39 – livelihood and, in 39(d), equal pay; Article 39A – added by the 42nd Amendment.
Article 41
covers the right to work, to education and to public assistance.
Article 36 – definition of 'State'; Article 43 – living wage; Article 49 – protection of monuments; Article 51 – international peace.
Articles 39A, 43A and 48A were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), and Article 45, once free education up to 14, now covers early childhood care after the 86th Amendment.
Article 46 concerns the promotion of the educational interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Article 40
directs the State to organise village panchayats.
Article 47 covers nutrition levels and prohibition of intoxicating drinks; Article 48 covers organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry (including cow protection).
Article 19
lists the six freedoms in clauses 19(1)(a) to 19(1)(g).
